```{r setup, include=FALSE}
grd_eval_docs <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = grd_eval_docs)
```

The methods in `griddy` come from the spatial distribution dynamics
literature, most directly the spatial Markov chain of Rey (2001) and the
homogeneity tests studied by Rey, Kang, and Wolf (2016). Their reference
implementation is PySAL [`giddy`](https://pysal.org/giddy/). `griddy`
implements the same methods in R, for long `sf` panels with tidy outputs.

`griddy` is not a port of `giddy`. It uses `giddy` as a validation oracle
rather than as a specification. Static fixtures from giddy 2.3.9 check the
classic and spatial Markov counts and probabilities, sojourn and
first-passage times, the mobility indices, and the Pearson and
likelihood-ratio homogeneity statistics. Some `giddy` features take only a
few lines of `griddy`, `sfdep`, `dplyr`, or base R, and are documented here as
recipes rather than added as functions.

This article maps every public entry of giddy 2.3.9 onto `griddy`.

## How to read the table

Each entry falls into one of four categories:

- **Implemented**: a `griddy` function covers it.
- **Composition**: there is no dedicated function, but a short recipe built
  from `griddy`, `sfdep`, `dplyr`, or base R produces the same result. The
  longer recipes are worked through [below](#worked-compositions), with
  checks against giddy 2.3.9 output.
- **Planned**: deliberately deferred to a later release.
- **Out of scope**: `griddy` does not intend to cover it. The table points to
  the tool that does.

The enumeration covers the `__all__` lists of the `markov`, `ergodic`,
`mobility`, `rank`, `directional`, `sequence`, and `util` modules. Where a
class has attributes or options with a different answer from the class as a
whole, they get their own row. The `giddy.plotting` functions belong to
`Rose` and are grouped with it. `giddy.components` is an internal helper for
`LISA_Markov.spillover()`.

## Coverage table

| giddy 2.3.9 | Category | In griddy, or where to go |
|:-------|:---|:------------|
| `markov.Markov`: `transitions`, `p` | Implemented | `markov_dynamics()`, `transition_matrix()`, with classes from `classify_dynamics()` |
| `markov.Markov`: `steady_state`, `mfpt`, `sojourn_time` | Implemented | `steady_state()`, `first_passage()`, `sojourn_time()` |
| `markov.Markov`: communicating, recurrent, and absorbing classes; multiple steady states of a reducible chain | Out of scope | The [`markovchain`](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=markovchain) package: `communicatingClasses()`, `recurrentClasses()`, `absorbingStates()`, `steadyStates()`. `griddy`'s chain summaries assume one recurrent class, and `first_passage()` requires an irreducible chain. |
| `markov.Markov(fill_empty_classes = True)` | Composition | `griddy` leaves rows with no departures as `NA`. To fill them: `P[is.na(P)] <- 0; diag(P)[rowSums(P) == 0] <- 1` ([recipe](#smaller-recipes)) |
| `markov.Spatial_Markov`: `T`, `P`, `transitions`, `p`; pooled classes (`fixed = True`); `k`, `m` | Implemented | `spatial_markov()` with `k` and `lag_k`, `transition_matrix(x, lag_class = ...)`, `class_intervals()`, `lag_intervals()` |
| `markov.Spatial_Markov`: `s`, `f`, `S`, `F` | Composition | `steady_state()` and `first_passage()` applied to `transition_matrix(x, lag_class = ...)` for each lag class; the aspatial `s` and `f` come from a `markov_dynamics()` chain ([recipe](#conditional-chain-summaries)) |
| `markov.Spatial_Markov`: `Q`, `LR`, `dof_hom`, `ht`, `summary()` | Implemented | `homogeneity_test()`, `chi2` and `likelihood_ratio` rows |
| `markov.Spatial_Markov`: `x2`, `x2_pvalue`, `x2_dof` | Implemented | `x2` is the same Pearson statistic as `Q`, the `chi2` row of `homogeneity_test()`. giddy tests `x2` against k(k − 1)² degrees of freedom; `homogeneity_test()` uses the Bickenbach and Bode count, as giddy does for `Q`. |
| `markov.Spatial_Markov`: `chi2` (one test per lag class); `markov.chi2()` | Composition | A short function on `transition_matrix(x, "count", lag_class = ...)` and the pooled counts ([recipe](#smaller-recipes)) |
| `markov.Spatial_Markov(fixed = False)`, `cutoffs`, `lag_cutoffs`, `discrete = True` | Composition | Value classes: `classify_dynamics(method = "time_quantile")` or `method = "fixed"` with `breaks`. Lag classes: join any per-unit, per-period regime to the `transitions` of a `markov_dynamics()` chain and count by it. Examples: a spatial lag cut at your own breaks or within each period, or the most common neighbouring class from `sfdep::find_xj()` ([recipe](#conditioning-on-any-regime)). |
| `markov.Spatial_Markov`: `shtest`; permutation inference (`permutations`, `x2_rpvalue`, `x2_realizations`) | Out of scope | Use `homogeneity_test()`. giddy's documentation advises caution with `shtest` and `chi2` and describes the permutation `x2` test as experimental. |
| `markov.LISA_Markov`: `q`, `transitions`, `p`, `steady_state`, `move_types`, `geoda_quads` | Composition | Quadrants from `sfdep::local_moran()` for each period, passed to `markov_dynamics()`. Move types are the `transition` column; GeoDa numbering is a relabelling of the factor levels ([recipe](#lisa-markov)). |
| `markov.LISA_Markov(permutations > 0)`: `p_values`, `significant_moves` | Composition | Join the permutation p-values from `sfdep::local_moran()` at the origin and destination periods to the chain's `transitions` |
| `markov.LISA_Markov`: `chi_2`, `expected_t` | Out of scope | `griddy` has no test that own and neighbour moves are independent. To test whether transitions differ by LISA quadrant, condition on the quadrant and use `homogeneity_test()` ([recipe](#lisa-markov)). |
| `markov.LISA_Markov.spillover()` | Out of scope | `spdep::subset.nb()` and `spdep::n.comp.nb()` find connected clusters among units with significant `sfdep::local_moran()` results, which is what it builds on |
| `markov.kullback()` | Implemented | `homogeneity_test()`, `kullback` row, which [differs on purpose](#giddy-differences) |
| `markov.homogeneity()`, `markov.Homogeneity_Results` | Implemented | `homogeneity_test()` on a list of regime count matrices |
| `markov.prais()` | Composition | `1 - diag(transition_matrix(x))`; the scalar Prais–Shorrocks index is `mobility_index(x, "prais")` |
| `markov.sojourn_time()` | Implemented | `sojourn_time()` |
| `markov.FullRank_Markov` | Planned | Until then, `classify_dynamics(method = "time_quantile", k = n)` followed by `markov_dynamics()` gives the same transition counts ([recipe](#rank-markov-chains)) |
| `markov.GeoRank_Markov` | Planned | Until then, `markov_dynamics()` with the within-period rank as `id` and the unit as `state` gives the same transition counts ([recipe](#rank-markov-chains)) |
| `ergodic.steady_state()` | Implemented | `steady_state()` |
| `ergodic.mfpt()`, deprecated `ergodic.fmpt()` | Implemented | `first_passage()`, for irreducible chains |
| `ergodic.var_mfpt_ergodic()`, deprecated `ergodic.var_fmpt_ergodic()` | Composition | Kemeny and Snell's variance formula, using `first_passage()`, `steady_state()`, and the fundamental matrix ([recipe](#smaller-recipes)) |
| `mobility.markov_mobility()` | Implemented | `mobility_index()`: `"P"`, `"D"`, `"L2"`, `"B1"`, `"B2"` are `"prais"`, `"determinant"`, `"eigen"`, `"bartholomew1"`, `"bartholomew2"` |
| `rank.Tau` | Composition | `stats::cor.test(x, y, method = "kendall")` returns the same tau-b. The asymptotic p-values differ slightly. |
| `rank.SpatialTau`, `rank.Tau_Local`, `rank.Tau_Local_Neighbor`, `rank.Tau_Local_Neighborhood`, `rank.Tau_Regional` | Planned | Spatial and local decompositions of Kendall's tau, including the local indicators of mobility association (LIMA) |
| `rank.Theta` | Composition | Rank each period with `rank()`, take each unit's rank change between adjacent periods, then compute `sum(abs(tapply(change, regime, sum))) / sum(abs(change))` for each pair of adjacent periods. Use `sample(regime)` for permutation inference. `rank_mobility()` gives tied values the minimum rank rather than the average, so it reproduces `Theta` only when there are no ties. |
| `directional.Rose`, its `permute()` and plot methods, and the `giddy.plotting` functions | Planned | Rose diagrams of directional LISA vectors |
| `sequence.Sequence` | Out of scope | [`TraMineR`](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=TraMineR): `seqdef()` and `seqdist()` with `method = "HAM"`, `"OM"`, or `"OMstran"`; transition-rate substitution costs come from `seqcost(method = "TRATE")` |
| `util.fill_empty_diagonals()` | Composition | As for `fill_empty_classes` above |
| `util.shuffle_matrix()` | Composition | `i <- sample(nrow(X)); X[i, i]` |
| `util.get_lower()` | Composition | `t(X)[upper.tri(X)]` returns the lower triangle in giddy's row-major order |

## Worked compositions {#worked-compositions}

The examples use the bundled `usjoin` panel of state per-capita income. The
geometry comes from `spData::us_states`, and its queen contiguity matches the
`states48.gal` weights in giddy's examples, so results can be compared with
giddy directly.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(griddy)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(sfdep)

data(usjoin)
data(us_states, package = "spData")

states <- us_states |>
  filter(NAME %in% usjoin$name) |>
  arrange(NAME) |>
  select(name = NAME) |>
  mutate(
    nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
    wt = st_weights(nb)
  )

panel <- usjoin |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(rel_income = income / mean(income)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  arrange(year, name)
```

### LISA Markov {#lisa-markov}

`sfdep::local_moran()` returns each unit's quadrant. Its `pysal` column uses
the same convention as giddy: the standardized value against its spatial lag.
Computing quadrants for each period and passing them to `markov_dynamics()`
gives the LISA Markov chain.

```{r}
set.seed(2001)
lisa_panel <- panel |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(quadrant = local_moran(income, states$nb, states$wt, nsim = 99)$pysal) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(quadrant = factor(
    quadrant,
    levels = c("High-High", "Low-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low")
  ))

lisa <- markov_dynamics(lisa_panel, name, year, quadrant)
transition_matrix(lisa, "count")
```

The counts match `giddy.markov.LISA_Markov` on the same data and weights:

```{r}
giddy_lisa_counts <- matrix(
  c(1087,   44,    4,  34,
      41,  470,   36,   1,
       5,   34, 1422,  39,
      30,    1,   40, 552),
  nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE
)
all.equal(as.vector(transition_matrix(lisa, "count")), as.vector(giddy_lisa_counts))
```

The result is an ordinary `grd_markov` object, so the chain summaries apply:

```{r}
steady_state(lisa)
sojourn_time(lisa)
```

To ask whether income-class transitions differ by LISA quadrant, condition on
the quadrant at the start of each transition and test homogeneity across
quadrants:

```{r}
income_chain <- classify_dynamics(lisa_panel, name, year, rel_income, k = 5) |>
  markov_dynamics(name, year, class)

by_quadrant <- income_chain$transitions |>
  left_join(
    lisa_panel |> select(id = name, from_time = year, quadrant),
    by = c("id", "from_time")
  )

quadrant_counts <- lapply(
  split(by_quadrant, by_quadrant$quadrant),
  function(d) table(d$from_state, d$to_state)
)
homogeneity_test(quadrant_counts)
```

### Conditioning on any regime {#conditioning-on-any-regime}

The quadrant example is a general pattern. Join any per-unit, per-period
regime to a chain's `transitions`, count by regime, and pass the list of count
matrices to `homogeneity_test()`. `spatial_markov()` uses the same pattern
with pooled quantiles of the spatial lag. Applying the pattern to its lag
classes reproduces its result:

```{r}
spatial <- spatial_markov(panel, name, year, rel_income, geometry = states, k = 5)

by_lag <- income_chain$transitions |>
  left_join(
    spatial$lag_panel |> select(id = name, from_time = year, lag_class),
    by = c("id", "from_time")
  )

lag_counts <- lapply(
  split(by_lag, by_lag$lag_class),
  function(d) table(d$from_state, d$to_state)
)
all.equal(homogeneity_test(lag_counts), homogeneity_test(spatial))
```

To use your own lag breaks, per-period lag quantiles, or a categorical lag,
replace `lag_class` in the join with that regime.

### Conditional chain summaries {#conditional-chain-summaries}

The conditional steady states and first-passage times (giddy's `S` and `F`)
come from applying the chain summaries to each lag class's matrix:

```{r}
conditional_steady_state <- sapply(
  spatial$lag_states,
  function(l) steady_state(transition_matrix(spatial, lag_class = l))
)
round(t(conditional_steady_state), 3)

first_passage(transition_matrix(spatial, lag_class = "Q1"))
```

### Rank Markov chains {#rank-markov-chains}

Full rank and geographic rank Markov chains are planned. In the meantime,
both can be built with existing functions. These reproduce the transition
counts of giddy's `FullRank_Markov` and `GeoRank_Markov` on `usjoin`. In
`griddy`, rank state `Q1` is the lowest income; giddy numbers ranks from the
highest.

```{r}
full_rank <- usjoin |>
  classify_dynamics(name, year, income, method = "time_quantile", k = 48) |>
  markov_dynamics(name, year, class)

geo_rank <- usjoin |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(rank = rank(income, ties.method = "first")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  markov_dynamics(rank, year, name)

dim(transition_matrix(full_rank))
dim(transition_matrix(geo_rank))
```

### Smaller recipes {#smaller-recipes}

Pearson tests of each lag class's counts against the pooled probabilities
(giddy's `markov.chi2()` and `Spatial_Markov.chi2`). Their sum is the `chi2`
row of `homogeneity_test()`:

```{r}
chi2_vs <- function(counts, reference) {
  expected <- rowSums(counts) * prop.table(reference, 1)
  expected[is.na(expected)] <- 0
  sum((counts - expected)^2 / ifelse(expected == 0, 1, expected))
}

pooled <- Reduce(`+`, lag_counts)
per_lag <- vapply(lag_counts, chi2_vs, numeric(1), reference = pooled)
per_lag

giddy_per_lag <- c(
  40.5598541260764, 55.4751973848766, 17.7528996233674,
  40.0390961477108, 46.7966803487369
)
all.equal(unname(per_lag), giddy_per_lag)
all.equal(sum(per_lag), homogeneity_test(spatial)$statistic[1])
```

Variances of first-passage times (Kemeny and Snell), checked against the
example in giddy's `var_mfpt_ergodic()` documentation:

```{r}
var_first_passage <- function(P) {
  k <- nrow(P)
  stat <- steady_state(P)
  Z <- solve(diag(k) - P + matrix(stat, k, k, byrow = TRUE))
  M <- first_passage(P)
  ZM <- Z %*% M
  W <- M %*% (2 * diag(diag(Z)) %*% diag(1 / stat) - diag(k)) +
    2 * (ZM - matrix(1, k, k) %*% diag(diag(ZM)))
  W - M * M
}

P <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0.5, 0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.25, 0.5), 3, byrow = TRUE)
var_first_passage(P)
```

Per-class Prais mobility (giddy's `markov.prais()`), filling rows with no
departures, and giddy's `util.get_lower()` ordering:

```{r}
1 - diag(transition_matrix(income_chain))

P <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.5, 0, NA, NA, NA, 0, 0.2, 0.8), 3, byrow = TRUE)
P[is.na(P)] <- 0
diag(P)[rowSums(P) == 0] <- 1
P

X <- matrix(c(0, 1, 2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 2, 2, 1, 0, 1, 4, 2, 1, 0), 4, byrow = TRUE)
t(X)[upper.tri(X)]
```

## Where griddy differs from giddy 2.3.9 {#giddy-differences}

There is one intentional difference. In `homogeneity_test()`, the `chi2` and
`likelihood_ratio` rows match giddy's `Spatial_Markov.Q` and
`Spatial_Markov.LR`. The `kullback` row does not match
`giddy.markov.kullback()` in giddy 2.3.9, for two reasons:

- It uses origin-state (row) margins for the stratum-specific term. giddy
  2.3.9 uses terminal-state margins, which
  [pysal/giddy#260](https://github.com/pysal/giddy/pull/260) fixes upstream.
- It uses the Bickenbach and Bode (2003) degrees of freedom instead of
  r(s − 1)(r − 1), which overstates the degrees of freedom when some
  transitions are never observed. See
  [pysal/giddy#265](https://github.com/pysal/giddy/issues/265).

With origin-state margins the Kullback statistic is algebraically the
likelihood-ratio statistic. With the same degrees of freedom, the `kullback`
row therefore equals the `likelihood_ratio` row. It is kept for comparability
with giddy. See the [NEWS](../news/index.html) entry for 0.2.0 and
`?homogeneity_test`.

Kemeny, J. G., and Snell, J. L. (1976). *Finite Markov Chains*. Springer.

Rey, S. J. (2001). Spatial empirics for economic growth and convergence.
*Geographical Analysis*, 33(3), 195–214.
<https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1538-4632.2001.tb00444.x>

Rey, S. J., Kang, W., and Wolf, L. (2016). The properties of tests for spatial
effects in discrete Markov chain models of regional income distribution
dynamics. *Journal of Geographical Systems*, 18(4), 377–398.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/s10109-016-0234-x>
